e: Latin alacritas, from alacer (lively, eager), which gave French allègre.
t: Alacer → « allègre »: accepting with alacrity = « avec empressement ».

e: Greek anathema (thing devoted to evil, accursed). The Church’s formal curse and excommunication.
t: « Jeter l’anathème »: cursed by the Church. Lying is anathema to her.

e: Greek apogaion (away from the earth): apo + gē. A moon’s farthest point from Earth.

m: A person who renounces a belief or party.
t: Standing away from the faith: « apostat ».

e: Variant of errant (wandering): an “arrant thief” was a roving outlaw; then just “notorious, utter”.
t: Arrant nonsense = « une pure absurdité ». « Un fieffé menteur ».
No artifice: opposite of artful (Common I).

m: To reduce the force or effect of.

t: Low (« bas »): base motives. Base metals vs noble ones.

m: To evade (beg the question = assume what is to be proved).
e: Middle English beggen; “beg the question” translates Latin petitio principii.
t: Begging the question = « une pétition de principe »: circular logic.

e: From Byzantium, whose imperial court was famous for complex intrigue and bureaucracy.
t: « Des querelles byzantines »: the labyrinthine Byzantine court.
Catholic tastes = eclectic, covering the whole (holos).
Chary = full of care, cautious: chary of giving out his number.

e: Greek kholērikos, from kholē (yellow bile), the humour of anger.

t: Behaving like a churl (lowly peasant): churlish to refuse.

m: Causing or likely to cause argument.

t: Cowed into silence: made meek as a cow.
Same as « défrayer »: travel costs defrayed.

m: To use ambiguous language to conceal the truth.
e: Late Latin aequivocare (to call by the same name).
Latin expungere (to prick out). Scribes marked deletions with dots.

t: Feck = effect. Feckless = without effect: the feckless flatmate who never pays his share.

m: Irritable and quarrelsome; hard to control.
e: From fraction in the old sense “discord”, Latin frangere (to break).
t: Breaking into factions: a fractious coalition.

m: To bully, talk to in an intimidating way.
e: From Hector of Troy; in 17th-c. London, “Hectors” were swaggering street bullies.
t: Hector of Troy: in 17th-century London, “hectors” were swaggering street bullies.
In + suffer: someone you cannot suffer (endure): « insupportable ».
The Victorian music-hall crowd singing for war.

m: To act in an excessively subservient way.
e: Chinese kòutóu (knock head): touching the forehead to the ground before the emperor.
t: Forehead on the floor before the emperor.

m: Feeling or showing overt sexual desire.
Wrongdoing, especially by a public official.

e: Arabic naẓīr (opposite), i.e. the point opposite the zenith.
t: Nadir = the point right under your feet, opposite the zenith above your head.

e: over + ween (to think, Old English wēnan). Thinking too much of oneself.
Tamil paraiyar, drummers at festivals, a caste treated as outcasts in colonial India.
Late Latin perfunctorius (careless), from perfungi (to get through, discharge).
t: Just getting it done: a perfunctory nod.

m: Slow and clumsy because heavy; dull.
To cause to happen suddenly; hasty.

e: From Saturn, the planet said by astrologers to make people gloomy.

t: Sedulous ≈ assiduous: steady, careful, persevering work.

e: Latin supercilium (eyebrow): raising the eyebrow in disdain.

m: A change of circumstances, usually unwelcome.
